entry.title: Nothing new. Exit code 0.
entry.summary: Originally published at tothenoc.substack.com A check that cannot fail is not a check. Last week a check told me there was nothing new in my mailbox. There were four messages that mattered, all from that same day. The check did not fail. It ran, it filtered, it returned an empty list. The filter compared dates written as text, and the text did not match. Empty, no error. I caught it by reading the mailbox myself. It was not the first time. Same family, different tools, all on our own systems: a search over the mail server returned zero results. The mailboxes are stored compressed. The search read the raw files, found nothing, and said so politely. an upgrade script exited with code 0, one second after it started. It had checked who was running it, did not like the answer, and quietly did nothing. a daily report came out as a file of zero bytes. Its output path pointed to a folder that had been archived the night before. None of these crashed. A crash is easy, somebody sees it. The dangerous result is the one that looks exactly like good news: nothing found, nothing changed, nothing to report. What we do now: every check has a positive control, a known item it must find. If the check cannot find the thing I know is there, its zero means nothing, a result that came back too fast is not a result. Zero hits on a full disk in zero seconds is a tool that did not look, read the log, not the exit code. Code 0 says the program ended. It does not say what it did, a report has a last line that says it finished. No last line, no report. "Nothing new" is a claim. Before you believe it, ask how the check would look if something was new. If you are deciding who watches this for you, this is what to ask: what an outsourced NOC actually covers, and what it costs. -- Alex

entry.summary: If you run Java workloads on Kubernetes, you have probably stared at slow pod readiness metrics during a deployment or autoscaling event. entry.title: Webhook signature verification fails even though the secret is right
entry.summary: Reproduced in my own test setup — not a client's, and no real account involved: The setup: a test endpoint receives the webhook, parses the JSON body, then What actually breaks it: the signature is computed over the exact bytes that The fix, in order: Capture the raw request body as bytes BEFORE any JSON parsing, and verify the signature against those bytes only. In most frameworks that means reading the raw body / disabling the JSON body parser on the webhook route. Only after verification passes, parse the body and process the event. If your platform parses the body for you before your code runs (some no-code webhook steps do), check whether it offers a "raw body" output — if it doesn't, verify at a step that still sees the raw payload, or move verification to a small endpoint that does. How to tell this apart from a genuinely wrong secret: compute the HMAC One gotcha while testing: don't "verify" by re-sending from a tool that re-serializes the payload for you — you'll reproduce the failure and conclude the secret is wrong. Test against the exact bytes the sender sent.
